                                              Message from the
                                         OSDI ’25 Program Co-Chairs
Welcome to the 18th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation (OSDI ’25).
We’re pleased to once again co-locate OSDI with the 2025 USENIX Annual Technical Conference (USENIX ATC ’25).
Together, these conferences present a broad and exciting collection of research papers, showcasing some of the most innova-
tive work in the systems community. We hope you leave with new ideas, new collaborators, and new friends.
This year, OSDI received 339 submissions, of which 48 were accepted with shepherding. In addition, 5 papers from Revise-
and-Resubmit track were later accepted, bringing the total to 53 papers included in the OSDI ’25 proceedings — an overall
acceptance rate of 16%. Three additional revise-and-resubmit papers are still under review and, if accepted, will appear in
next year’s OSDI ’26 proceedings.
OSDI remains a single-track conference, allowing attendees to engage fully with every paper presented. We’ve organized a
three-day program where all presentations are held in a single room, encouraging shared discussion and broad exposure to
the entire program.
To fairly and thoroughly evaluate submissions across the wide range of topics OSDI covers, we assembled a program com-
mittee of 92 expert reviewers (not including the two of us as co-chairs). Reviewing such a large volume of high-quality
research is no small task. Each paper received at least three reviews in the first round. A select group of papers advanced to a
second round and received two or three additional reviews. We then held an intensive online discussion period followed by a
two-day program committee meeting.
In total, the committee produced more than 1,500 reviews and thousands of discussion comments. We deeply appreciate the
thoughtful and constructive feedback provided by the program committee. Reviewers also need to conduct additional reviews
for revise-and-resubmit papers. Their careful assessments helped ensure that the selected papers reflect the best of what the
systems community has to offer. Each accepted paper was assigned a shepherd from the committee to help the authors refine
their work based on reviewer feedback, and we’re proud of the clarity and quality of the final versions. We also extend our
sincere thanks to the small group of external reviewers who generously contributed their expertise when additional perspec-
tives were needed.
We also want to recognize the contributions of the Artifact Evaluation Committee, which was shared between OSDI and
USENIX ATC. Co-chaired by Ryan Huang and Tianyin Xu—both of whom also served as OSDI ’25 program committee
members—this team assessed the supporting artifacts submitted with papers. Their work plays a key role in promoting repro-
ducibility and encouraging rigorous experimental methods. One paper this year was recognized with a Distinguished Artifact
Award.
The poster session at OSDI ’25 was organized by Patrick P. C. Lee and Chen Li, who also served on the program committee.
They coordinated the submission and selection process for this session, which includes posters from both accepted papers
and additional research contributions. The poster session offers another opportunity for attendees to exchange ideas and con-
nect with the broader systems community.
Once the accepted papers were decided, we began the process of deciding on the Jay Lepreau Best Paper Awards. A small
committee of non-conflicted Program Committee members—excluding both program co-chairs— read all of the top-ranked
and PC-nominated papers and made the final decision on the award papers. We sincerely thank the best paper selection com-
mittee for their thoughtful evaluations and dedication to recognizing outstanding contributions to the community—especially
within a tight timeframe.
We are incredibly grateful to the many people who contributed to this conference. To the authors: thank you for submitting
your work and for your dedication to pushing systems research forward. To the program committee and external reviewers:
thank you for your time, expertise, and thoughtful evaluations. Special thanks to Eric Mugnier from UCSD and Carol Zhang
from Microsoft Research for their behind-the-scenes help in the PC meeting, including conflict tracking and note-taking.
We also thank the USENIX staff for their exceptional support and professionalism. Their experience and coordination behind
the scenes made the organizational process smoother at every step—from paper submissions to final conference.
Finally, thank you to all attendees. Conferences like OSDI thrive because of your participation, your questions, and your
collaboration. We hope you enjoy the program, reconnect with colleagues, and discover new ideas and directions in systems
research.
It has been an honor to serve as the Program Co-Chairs for OSDI ’25. Thank you for trusting us with this role, and we hope
the conference is rewarding and inspiring for you.
Warm regards,
Lidong Zhou
Yuanyuan (YY) Zhou
OSDI ’25 Program Co-Chairs

Table 1: User experience metrics of Basilisk compared to Kondo. A lower number is better for every column, and the shaded
cells under Kondo highlight areas where it is outperformed by Basilisk. ‘Size’ counts the lines of code the user writes to express
the protocol. ‘User invs’ is the number of invariant clauses that the user manually supplies. ‘Mono annots’ is the number of
monotonic type annotations the user writes—these numbers are identical between Basilisk and Kondo. ‘Lines of proof’ is the
amount of proof code the user writes to complete the safety proof. In both Basilisk and Kondo, ‘Safety’ is the size of the Dafny
lemmas used to prove safety, while ‘Total’ includes additional definitions of proof obligations. In Kondo, ‘Total’ also includes
the definitions of manually-written invariants, which Basilisk does not require. Finally, ‘Time’ is the time Dafny takes to verify
the final proof of the history-preserving asynchronous protocol.

Distributed Lock. Hosts pass around a single lock in a ring
configuration [10].
   Safety property: At most one host holds the lock at any
instant.

ShardedKV. A sharded key-value store where a shard may
transfer a key to another shard.
   Safety property: Every key is owned by at most one host.

ShardedKV-Batched. Same as the ShardedKV, except keys
may be transferred in arbitrary-sized batches.
  Safety property: Every key is owned by at most one host.

Lock Server. A single server host may grant a lock to one
of many client hosts, and clients may return a lock it holds
back to the server [21].
   Safety property: At most one client holds the lock at any
instant.

Two-Phase Commit. The classic Two-Phase Commit pro-
tocol.
   Safety property: The conjunction of
 1. All processes that reach a decision reach the same deci-
    sion as the coordinator,
 2. The Commit decision can only be reached if all processes
    prefer Yes, and
 3. if all processes prefer Yes, then the decision must be
    Commit.

SR-IOV and I/O device passthrough enable network and
storage devices to be shared among multiple tenants with                   Reclaimable by VIO: 120GB

native performance. However, passthrough does not support
page faults, requiring the hypervisor to statically pin the VM-
allocated memory. This approach is unacceptable for cloud
service providers (CSPs) that rely on oversubscription to en-              Legacy VM Memory: 800GB
hance memory utilization and reduce costs. The Page Request
Interface (PRI) was designed to support device-side I/O page
faults (IOPFs) through collaboration among devices, Input-
Output Memory Management Units (IOMMU), and the OS.                        Other: 200GB
But PRI has not seen broad adoption in devices like NICs and
storage.

                                                                  6.3    Future Work
6     Discussion                                                  The VirtIO 1.1 standard draft, introduced in 2018, offers the
                                                                  Packed virtqueue as a more efficient alternative to the Split
                                                                  virtqueue [1]. Future iterations of VIO are planned to support
6.1    Compatibility                                              VirtIO 1.1, further improving I/O efficiency and scalability.

In this paper, we present a Linux-based implementation of
VIO, which ensures high compatibility for several key reasons.    7     Conclusion
First, VIO is built upon the VirtIO interface, a standardized
virtual I/O interface that is supported across various CPU        This paper presents VIO, a production-level I/O virtualiza-
architectures and does not depend on specific hardware I/O        tion framework offering hardware independence, high perfor-
devices or kernel versions. This makes the implementation         mance, and resource efficiency. VIO introduces: 1) an elastic
highly portable and flexible. Second, VIO does not require        passthrough mechanism adapting to IOPS demands for near-
any modifications to the guest OS, as it operates transparently   native performance; 2) an adaptive lockpage mechanism re-
through the VirtIO interface. This ensures that VIO maintains     ducing IOPFs by pinning frequently accessed pages; and 3) a
full compatibility with a wide range of guest OSes, includ-       proactive snooping approach separating IOPF handling from
ing Linux, BSD, and even Windows, without enforcing any           the critical I/O path. Unlike PRI, which struggles with latency
changes or additional dependencies. In theory, VIO can work       and limited hardware adoption, VIO provides a practical and
with other hypervisors like Xen, Firecracker which supports       efficient solution for large-scale cloud environments.
VirtIO for efficient I/O virtualization. Moreover, VIO’s design      VIO, deployed across 300K VMs, achieves up to the equiv-
leverages basic virtualization features of the system, ensuring   alent of 30K VM memory daily savings while maintaining
broad hardware compatibility. CPU platforms, including Pow-       I/O SLOs with less than 1% IOPFs compared to CPU page
erPC, ARM, and RISC-V, can theoretically support VIO, as          faults, demonstrating its efficiency and scalability in produc-
they widely adopt VirtIO in their virtualization ecosystems.      tion environments.

USENIX Association                            19th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation           99
receiving data, ML processes indicate receiving buffers and
get notified from proxy threads when the data is ready.
   We intercept proxy thread function calls to interact with
FuseLink, including connection establishment, network buffer
registration, and sending/receiving data.
Connection establishment. Instead of building raw RDMA
connections, we modify proxy threads by posting connection
request to FuseLink, which handles the request by setting
up connections through multiple NICs within the server. Af-
ter connection setup, proxy threads get connection ids that
are used to post sending and receiving operations. All net-
work operations are conducted by posting control messages         Figure 9: Average inter-server GPU bandwidth achieved by a
to FuseLink with the connection id.                               single GPU when using different numbers of NICs
Registering buffers. By default, NCCL registers buffers on
the specified device to enable RDMA NICs to access network
buffers. We modify proxy threads to expose network buffers to
FuseLink, which remaps buffers to relay GPUs and registers
network buffers on RDMA NIC. Since each buffer only needs
to be registered once in the NIC, remapping to relays brings
minor overhead. Note that FuseLink maps network buffers
back to original GPUs when NIC contention arises. Thus, we
register network buffers on relay GPUs and original GPUs to
avoid repeated registration. The registered memory regions
are selected based on the current GPU to which the network
buffer is mapped.

   Despite the similarity of using intermediate GPUs,              9   Conclusion
FuseLink has three key differences compared to PXN. First,
PXN binds traffic to intermediate GPUs and statically copies       In this paper, we present FuseLink to enable inter-server GPUs
data to GPUs. This can only improve one NIC throughput,            to efficiently communicate over multiple NICs. FuseLink ex-
yet others are in suboptimal PCIe connections. In contrast,        ploits dedicated intra-server network for intra-server traffic
FuseLink dynamically integrates NVLink interconnect in the         routing to fully utilize GPU interconnects when communicat-
network data path. Consequently, FuseLink can fully elimi-         ing through NICs. FuseLink achieves improved inter-server
nate the suboptimal PCIe data path on multiple NICs during         bandwidth without interrupting ongoing computation and
inter-server communication. Second, FuseLink identifies and        communication tasks on peer GPUs. Through our evaluation,
leverages idle NICs, while PXN is configured statically by         we verify that FuseLink is effective in dynamic-traffic ma-
NCCL, given the system topology before running communica-          chine learning tasks, achieving high inter-server GPU band-
tion tasks. Finally, FuseLink achieves higher inter-server band-   width and accelerating machine learning tasks including LLM
width for GPU communication by utilizing multiple NICs,            serving, EP MoE training, and DLRM training.
while PXN is bounded by the single NIC bandwidth.

    Yibo Huang, Haowei Chen, Newton Ni, Yan Sun† , Vijay Chidambaram, Dixin Tang, Emmett Witchel

                           Abstract                                   distributed transaction processing [4, 13, 20, 21, 32, 62, 71–73].
                                                                      Many papers adopt an RDMA-based shared and disaggre-
Building efficient distributed transactional databases remains
                                                                      gated memory architecture to avoid multi-partition transac-
a challenging problem despite decades of research. Existing

5     Related Work                                                  This paper introduces Tigon, the first distributed in-memory
                                                                    database that synchronizes cross-host concurrent data accesses
CXL-enabled memory tiering. A lot of recent work on CXL             via atomic operations on CXL memory. Tigon addresses the
memory management focuses on system software moving                 inherent limitations of CXL memory, including higher latency,
memory pages between local and CXL memory on behalf of              lower bandwidth, and limited hardware support for cache
applications [22, 54, 59, 65, 83]. Much of the work focuses on      coherence, through three key innovations: a novel software
accurate detection of hot pages and policies for moving pages.      cache coherence protocol for extending the cache-coherent
Some hot pages only contain a few hot lines [63], making            region, efficient concurrency control protocols for maintaining
it difficult to recoup the cost of migration and motivating         and accessing data in CXL memory, and a scalable logging
systems where hardware migrates cachelines [83].                    protocol for avoiding two-phase commit. Tigon is publicly
CXL-enabled memory pooling and sharing. Recent work                 available at https://github.com/ut-datasys/tigon.
explores how CXL-enabled memory pooling and sharing can
reduce cost in datacenters and HPC systems [11,28,45,70], ben-
efit serverless computing [28, 57], and accelerate distributed
applications [50, 51, 81]. Distributed applications sharing         7    Acknowledgment

                                                                       10    Conclusion
Distributed systems within the datacenter. Many works
improve the performance of distributed transactions within a           This paper presents Mako, a highly-available, fast, and scal-
datacenter [4,9,10,17,25,46,67,74,84,90,103,107,110,112].              able transactional database system, specifically optimized for
These systems use advanced hardware, such as HTM, RDMA,                geo-replication. Mako decouples transaction execution and
and DPDK, to deliver good performance, strong consistency,             replication, makes execution speculative, and leverages multi-
and fault tolerance. A key feature shared by these systems             core machines. Our experimental evaluation shows that Mako
is that replication happens side-by-side with transaction ex-          outperforms state-of-the-art geo-replicated transactional sys-
ecution and/or commit, making transaction backup part of               tems by an order of magnitude in throughput.
the critical path. In contrast, Mako is specifically optimized
for geo-replicated databases and can therefore withstand full

achieving high performance through speculative execution.              We thank the anonymous reviewers for suggestions that im-

epoch or from invalid shards (e.g., those deleted in the new      driven strategy for managing helper threads responsible for
configuration).                                                   processing RPC requests from other shard leaders, thereby
   Shard leaders then begin executing most transactions spec-     saving CPU resources. This approach entails temporarily sus-
ulatively, with two constraints: (1) keys must be below their     pending threads and resuming them when required, which
current view of vector watermarks to avoid potential data loss,   regrettably results in additional latency. Despite this trade-
and (2) keys scheduled for migration cannot be accessed to        off, the event-driven method can efficiently allocate CPU
ensure safety in the event of a shard failure during the shard    resources and preserve the overall system performance. In our
management. Since there is no need for all vector clocks from     implementation, we use two polling server threads that contin-
the old epoch to compare with new epoch vector clocks, elim-      uously receive DPDK messages and delegate those messages
inating concerns about mismatches between vector clocks           to the corresponding threads for execution. Mako’s RPC relies
across epochs.                                                    on eRPC [45] and a private RPC library.
   In the background, shards in the old configuration close the
old epoch and exchange shard watermarks to compute a FVW.
This process removes the first constraint, and the computed
FVW is persisted in the CM for future retrieval, eliminating
the need for independent recomputation.
   Simultaneously, each shard migrates key-value pairs to
other configured shards while retaining the original copies.
Once a shard completes its migration task, it reports back to
the CM. A background thread reclaims the original copies
only after the migration tasks for all shards are complete.
Shards marked for deletion are only responsible for closing
Paxos streams in the old epoch.
   When all migration tasks are completed, the CM issues a
MIGRATE-END RPC, lifting the second constraint and en-
abling full transaction execution under the new configuration.
In the event of a shard failure during the migration procedure,
the CM initiates a failure recovery procedure, assigning a new
epoch. After recovery, the CM can safely restart migration
procedure from the beginning.


C    Implementations
Multi-version and lazy memory de-allocation. As described
in the paper, Mako stores multiple versions of each key to
support rollbacks in shard failures. This is implemented as
a linked list. Each version contains a pointer to the previous
version on this key. The key index stores the pointer to the
latest version. We choose this implementation for the multi-
version to enable more efficient rollbacks. When rolling back
due to shard failures, the operation often requires reclaiming
memory for all versions that are incomparable to or above the
FVW of the old epoch, which can be very expensive. Instead,
Mako defers this operation to the future, usually the next
time the key is accessed. In our experience, we find this is an
engineering effort that can greatly reduce the rollback time.
Note that, some unnecessary rollbacks remain unavoidable
due to the lack of fine-grained dependency tracking between
individual transactions, which would incur high overhead.
Event-driven helper threads. In Mako, the limitation of
available CPUs makes it impractical to maintain a large num-
ber of busy-polling server threads simultaneously for receiv-
ing DPDK messages. As a solution, Mako adopts an event-

In this section, we introduce two types of related work, namely
graph search optimization and on-disk ANNS.
Graph search optimization. Traditional graph-based in-                7   Conclusion
dexes do ANNS in memory. They typically use greedy search
to traverse from the starting vector to the target vector [6, 16].    We propose PipeSearch, a low-latency algorithm for on-disk
Compared to distance comparison, memory access for vectors            graph-based ANNS. PipeSearch accelerates on-disk ANNS
has orders of magnitude lower latency, so the greedy-based ap-        by aligning the best-first search algorithm with SSD fea-
proach is favored for reduced vectors accessed per search. In         tures. It benefits from compute-I/O overlapping and a better-
such a scenario, distance comparison is the major bottleneck          utilized I/O pipeline compared to best-first search. We op-
of graph-based ANNS, so some works focus on reducing the              timize PipeSearch and implement PipeANN, a low-latency

                                                                     RGD semantics allow Skybridge to be minimal in size
                                                                  while still providing staleness information about recent writes
                                                                  in real time. Skybridge takes full advantage of its core princi-
                                                                  ples (only replicate metadata, known data loss, out-of-order
                                                                  replication, decoupling from Wormhole) to drastically boost
                                                                  TAO’s 2-second bounded staleness up to 99.99998%. It is
                                                                  able to achieve these benefits while helping TAO avoid going
                                                                  upstream for 99.9996% of queries. Skybridge is a reliable and
                                                                  efficient means for boosting TAO’s user experience.

                                                                  6   Limitations and future work
                                                                  Increased retention. Skybridge’s indexes are memory capac-
                                                                  ity bound and only cover several minutes’ worth of replication
       (a) Skybridge replication lag at P99, P99.9 and P99.99
                                                                  lag. Increasing the number of hosts or memory capacity per
                                                                  host would boost retention. Another strategy would be to
                                                                  spill older sections of indexes onto disk (e.g., flash drives).
                                                                  This would allow Skybridge to expand retention into the tens
                                                                  of minutes range but would require care to avoid regressing
                                                                  query latency. Other systems like Memcached [20] are able
                                                                  to support disk storage with minimal regressions, meaning it
                                                                  is likely a feasible solution for Skybridge.
                                                                     Dynamic sharding. TAO statically assigns data to shards,
                                                                  but systems like Cockroach DB [33], BigTable [12], Span-
                                                                  ner [16] and TiDB [28] are able to dynamically reshard data
                                                                  to balance load. Skybridge’s leasing mechanism could be
                                                                  extended to handle dynamic resharding, but would likely re-
                                                                  quire integration with the resharding control plane to safely
       (b) Skybridge latency at P50, P95 and P99 percentiles      coordinate changes.
                                                                     Global secondary indices. Meta uses global secondary
  Figure 7: Skybridge replication and query performance           indices [9] to materialize queries that would require many

programming models. The transcompiler consists of two parts: (a) neural-symbolic program synthesis, which utilizes LLM to transform
code and repair incorrect transformation through symbolic synthesis with limited scales, and (b) hierarchical performance auto-tuning, which
systemically explores both the parameters and sequences of transformation passes.

                                                                                                                 8   Conclusion and Future Work
                                                                                                                 Autoscaling is the key to achieving both high goodput and
7                 Related work                                                                                   hardware utilization in model as a service systems, but the
Optimizing model serving without autoscaling. Serving                                                            performance overhead introduced by current slow and stop-
models at scale is non-trivial. A significant body of research                                                   the-world autoscaling significantly limits its effectiveness.
focuses on how to efficiently utilize GPUs to accelerate                                                         In this paper, we first show that the data plane of model au-
model serving [81, 75, 44, 45, 77, 55, 31, 68], e.g., Orca [77]                                                  toscaling can be made fast with less than O(1) caching by
proposes iterative-scheduling and selective batching. Al-                                                        leveraging network-based model-aware multicast. We next
phaServe [45] employs pipeline parallelism to better handle                                                      show that the data plane can be made live through model-
load spikes, but it cannot adjust pipeline instances dynami-                                                     aware remote execution. Equipped with these two techniques,
cally. These systems assume running on a fixed pool of GPUs,                                                     our system B LITZ S CALE has at most 94.1 % better perfor-
and we have shown the necessity of dynamically adjusting                                                         mance and 19.46 % better resource utilization compared to
pool size and how to achieve so efficiently with B LITZ S CALE.                                                  state-of-the-art serving systems with and without autoscaling,
B LITZ S CALE complements these single-instance model serv-                                                      respectively. We believe our work demonstrates the poten-
ing systems with fast autoscaling mechanisms: we build upon                                                      tial and practicability of autoscaling-empowered model as a
them for fast model serving on a single instance, and addi-                                                      service systems.
tionally provide ultra-fast scaling when the system needs to                                                        While fast and live autoscaling of B LITZ S CALE takes
change the number of serving instances.                                                                          a key step toward modern elastic serving systems, several
Dynamic scaling serving instances. Dynamically scaling                                                           challenges remain. First, during our investigations, we found
serving instances is challenging, mainly because the size of                                                     scaling policies—determining when and how to scale—may
model weights is huge and still increasing, so loading them                                                      also impact system efficiency. The policy depends heavily
to the accelerators (data plane) is time-consuming. Some                                                         on workload characteristics, which we leave as future work.
existing works accelerate the loading [15, 41, 46, 62]: For                                                      Second, B LITZ S CALE currently focuses on instance-level
example, both PipeSwitch [15] and DeepPlan [41] leverage                                                         scaling, whereas modern models can scale by changing the
the layer-by-layer character of models to overlap the infer-                                                     parallel configuration within an instance, e.g., scaling experts
ence and parameter loading to hide the loading cost. They                                                        in mixture-of-experts (MoE) models. While B LITZ S CALE
only focus on host-to-device loading and such overlap is not                                                     in principle works for such a setup, we leave the detailed

6     Limitations                                                      Invariant Mining Much work has explored mining likely
                                                                       program invariants for traditional single-component software
T RAIN C HECK has a few limitations. First, its instrumenta-
                                                                       with tools such as Daikon [16] and DIDUCE [19]. These
tion interferes with JIT compilation tools like torch.compile,
                                                                       invariants focus on low-level program variable relations at
preventing the analysis of optimized code paths. Second, it
                                                                       certain points of the program, such as idx < len for two local
is restricted to Python code, limiting its ability to analyze
                                                                       variables in a loop. Recent work such as I4 [30], DistAI [49],
components with significant logic implemented in lower-level
                                                                       and DuoAI [48] infer inductive invariants, which are used in
languages, such as the Flash Attention algorithm [11]. Finally,
                                                                       the verification of distributed protocols. Oathkeeper [29] in-
representing tensors in hash form prevents fine-grained numer-
                                                                       fers event rules to detect silent failures in distributed systems.
ical analysis, limiting its applicability to detecting instabilities
caused by inappropriate hyperparameters. However, this can                Inferring rules is a general approach for bug detection. En-
be complemented by existing research on hyperparameter                 gler et al. [15] notably propose inferring rules about program-
tuning [50] and numerical defect detection [25].                       mer beliefs and show its effectiveness in large systems code.

failures across diverse training pipelines.
Monitoring Frameworks for Training Dynamics Tools                      Silent errors are detrimental to DL training and yet notoriously
like TensorBoard [1] and Weights & Biases [5] log high-level           difficult to address. This paper presents a study on such errors
metrics such as loss and accuracy, enabling developers to              to understand their characteristics. Informed by the study, we
visualize and compare experiments easily. However, these               propose a principle approach that uses precise training invari-
tools require manual and active monitoring, as seen during             ants to detect and diagnose silent training errors. We present
the training of BloombergGPT [45], where loss plateaued for            T RAIN C HECK, an end-to-end framework that automates the
seven days before the developer noticed it. These metrics are          process of inferring training invariants and proactively check-
often noisy and can lead to many false alarms when used for            ing them. T RAIN C HECK shows effective and quick detection
detecting silent errors. They also do not help with diagnosis.         capability for real-world silent training errors with diverse
   In contrast, T RAIN C HECK provides an automated solution           root causes. It also uncovers previously unknown bugs lead-
that captures the precise semantics of training as training in-        ing to silent errors in popular training libraries. Its tailored
variants and proactively checks them, enabling reduced man-            approach and the transferability of its inferred invariants make
ual effort, early and accurate detection of silent training errors,    it readily applicable to existing DL training pipelines.
and providing diagnosis hints for root-cause analysis.

     N EUTRINO: Fine-grained GPU Kernel Profiling via Programmable Probing

                              Songlin Huang                                  Chenshu Wu
                        The University of Hong Kong                   The University of Hong Kong

                          Abstract
    As GPUs play an increasingly important role in computer
systems in the scaling laws era, understanding fine-grained
GPU runtime behavior is more crucial than ever. However,
existing GPU kernel profilers, typically kernel-exclusive or
hardware-dependent, often fail to capture fine-grained mea-
surements. This paper presents N EUTRINO, a programmable
interface for GPU kernel profiling that leverages assembly-
layer probing to achieve instruction-level fine granularity, pro-
filing versatility across time and value domains, and hardware
independence. To better visualize the rich details captured
by N EUTRINO, we introduce the Densified Memory Access
Timeline (DMAT), a novel representation that offers new in-
sights into GPU runtime behavior. We implement N EUTRINO
in Linux for both NVIDIA and AMD GPUs and conduct                   Figure 1: N EUTRINO’s Densified Memory Access Timeline
extensive evaluations and analyses. The results demonstrate         Plot. ●

with low overhead. We envision N EUTRINO as a valuable              ware profilers. Color depth in ●
                                                                                                   A shows density from parallel
tool for the community and have open-sourced it to facilitate       threads, profiled from Flash-Attn-v2 [19] (non-causal).

neutrino.

2     Background and Design Choice
GPU Profiling: Profiling builds roadmaps for performance
engineering. Different from CPU profiling [12, 18] empha-
sizing sequential execution efficiency like branch prediction,
GPU profiling prioritizes parallel execution scalability like
compute unit utilization and throughput. Taking memory ac-
cess as an example, CPU profiling cares about temporal lo-
cality like the working set [22], while GPU profiling focuses
more on coalescing access among threads to utilize the band-
width, opening unique challenges and research opportunities.
GPU Ecosystem: In modern computer systems, GPU has
become a general-purpose computing unit (GPGPU) backed
by a huge and complicated ecosystem covering numerous                                                            Figure 2: Complex GPU Ecosystem divided in two branches
computing tasks, such as deep learning training [8, 27, 79]                                                      AOT (left) and JIT (right) unified at parallel assembly layer.
and inference [62, 94, 96]. However, from the perspective
of compilation, the complicated ecosystem can roughly be
divided into two branches: ❶ Ahead-of-Time (AOT) compiled                                                        chronization. Finally, blocks are grouped into grids mapped
operator libraries of hand-written codes [53] compiled by                                                        to the same GPU, which is the management unit for host side,
C++ compilers [6, 54], e.g., ATen [8]; ❷ Just-in-Time (JIT)                                                      and the measurement unit for kernel-exclusive profilers [87].
compiled domain-specific languages (DSLs) such as triton                                                            Similarly, the GPU memory is also hierarchically organized.
[91] compiled by LLVM [44] / MLIR [45]. As shown in                                                              First, each thread holds private registers (RMEM, at most 255

assembly. Consequently, to build a general-purpose profiler,                                                     have CU-level shared memory (SMEM, at most 164KB on
it has to be on or below the parallel assembly layer.                                                            A100) as the temporary buffer for results and communications.

highly limited. GPU programs are of direct execution without
a management layer like the OS kernel. Particularly, there is
no support for timer interrupts, a crucial feature for sampling-
based profilers. Therefore, profiling techniques on traditional
OSs, e.g., sampling and scanning the stack frame, are not
applicable to GPUs. Moreover, there are no commonly sup-
ported disk I/Os, making it troublesome to save results.
Assembly as a Probing Interface: The unique characteristics
of GPU programming pose great challenges in building N EU -
TRINO, a fine-grained, versatile, and programmable GPU pro-
filing tool that is kernel-inclusive and hardware-independent.
The key question we need to answer is: at which layer should
N EUTRINO be built and how? In this paper, among all the
choices in Fig. 2, we choose the parallel assembly, such as
PTX/GCNAsm [4, 60] designed to adapt to rapid changes in
system and machine code, as the probing interface. Impor-
tantly, instead of static approaches, such as customizing profil-
ing passes [21] via compilers or naive asm() in C, we employ
a more capable but challenging approach, attaching probe(s)

at runtime, which minimizes usage overhead (e.g., recompil-

choice not only allows forward- and backward-compatibility,

3.4    Verification for Security
Verification [28, 84] has been proven vital for programmable
probes [24] as unsafe probes can break the execution flow of
the original program and invalidate the profiling. The verifier
can also help guide developers in writing correct probes. In
N EUTRINO, we identify and prevent three key security issues:
Overwrite Original Registers: As discussed in §3.2, GPU
threads use registers as primary resources. Thus, modifica-
tions of registers used by the original program are unsafe. For   Figure 7: N EUTRINO workflow. Entry loads and JIT compiles
example, modifying a register holding address to global mem-      (§4.3) probes, and injects hook driver. Hook driver (§4.1) cap-
ory could lead to illegal memory access (Fig. 6A). Thus, N EU -   tures GPU workloads, invokes probe engine (§4.2), allocates
TRINO requires probes to use independent register groups, and     probe buffers, launches probed kernel, and dumps results.
prohibit probes that modify original registers.

                                                                               8   Discussion and Future Work
                                                                               N EUTRINO and GPU Scheduling: While we demonstrate
                                                                               the significance of N EUTRINO in revealing new insights
                                                                               from the runtime scheduling behavior in §4.6 and §7, cur-
                                                                               rent experiments are still far from completely understanding
                                                                               or reverse-engineering the GPU scheduling policies. This is
                                                                               because GPU scheduling is hardware-implemented, unlike
                                                                               OS schedulers like CFS or EEVDF [83,97], and is multi-level,
                                                                               including stream-, block-, and the finest warp-level instruction
                                                                               scheduling. Moreover, as a shared system, the behavior of the
                                                                               scheduler will be highly affected by runtime dynamics, which
                                                                               can also be reflected by the randomness of DMAT.

meet the needs of developers. For example, hardware profil-
ers can only profile the entire program in a sampling-based        The rapid development of AI systems has fostered an urgent
manner with low sampling frequency to control overhead in          need for comprehensive insights through advanced GPU ker-
performance and resources, limiting its capability to trace        nel profiling. To address this, we present N EUTRINO, a GPU
user-specified events. Instead, N EUTRINO limits the profil-       assembly probing infrastructure that enables fine-grained, ver-
ing targets to only the desired tracepoints, achieving both        satile, and programmable GPU kernel runtime profiling with
fine-grained event tracing and low system overhead.                its distinct probe design of snippet, tracepoint, and map. We
GPU Software Profiler: Other framework-specific software           implement N EUTRINO, consisting of the hook driver, probe
profilers, such as the built-in profiler of PyTorch [87] and       engine, and DSL compiler, for the CUDA and ROCm ecosys-
JAX [27], are kernel-exclusive and can only capture higher-        tems. We introduce the novel Densified Memory Access Time-
level events, like measuring memory events (alloc/free)            line (DMAT) to effectively visualize comprehensive GPU
or timing the whole kernel (FLOP/s). Instead, N EUTRINO            memory access patterns. We conduct extensive experiments,
focuses on intra-kernel profiling at the instruction level.        validating N EUTRINO’s reliability, low overhead, and applica-

ware design, GPU micro-benchmarking [1,38,51,64,85] tries          of synchronization, successfully pinpointing performance bot-
to profile the idealized performance of specific hardware via      tlenecks with new insights gained by N EUTRINO. To maxi-
specially designed workloads that only consist of interested       mize the potentials of N EUTRINO, we have open-sourced it at
instructions, such as mma to benchmark tensor core, without        https://github.com/open-neutrino/neutrino and plan

               1 NEVE [44]           Coalesce and defer traps to the hypervisor by logging to avoid context switch overhead between a VM and the hypervisor.
  Batching




               2 EAW [13]            Exclude outdated data from the batch by allowing modifications in the log before committing.
               3 IX [11]             Apply batching at every stage of the network stack, including system calls and hardware queues to enhance instruction and data locality.
               4 Drizzle [60]        Reuse scheduling decisions across micro-batches as computation is largely static and undergoes infrequent changes.
  Caching




               5 Protean [27]        Cache previous virtual machine allocation result and reuse the placement across multiple requests.
               6 Tasi et al. [58]    Decouple permission checking from locating a directory and memoizes permission check resuls to enable fast path.
               7 NetCache [32]       Let programmable switches to cache hot data for key-value store architectures.
               8 Duet [9]            Reorder storage maintenance to prioritize data already cached in memory.
 Precom-
  puting




               9 Itasks [18]         Proactively trigger memory reclaiming upon detecting the first sign of memory pressure to reduce garbage collection during critical path.
               10 Correctables [26] Prefetch dependent objects based on preliminary view instead of waiting for fully consistent one to hide the latency of strong consistency.
               11 Sparrow [51]       Delay assignment of tasks to worker machine until workers are prepared, mitigating race conditions among multiple distributed schedulers.
  Deferring




               12 PACTree [35]       With optimistic version lock, perform an operation optimistically without holding a lock and then check the version number.
               13 SKYROS [23]        Defer expensive ordering and operation execution until their effects are externalized.
               14 KnightKing [65]    Allow for sampling the next edge in random walk algorithms without scanning all out-edges at the walker’s current vertex.
  Relaxation




               15 RSS and RSC [28] Relax certain real-time guarantees of strict serializability for causally unrelated transactions or operations.
               16 SAUCR [6]          Relax durability and availability when most servers crash simultaneously to achieve performance comparable to memory-durable one.
               17 MemLiner [61]      Let application threads notify garbage collection tracing threads about accessed objects for better alignment of memory accesses.
 ualization
 Context-




               18 Syrup [34]         Use eBPF to have customized scheduling policies defined by applications.
               19 CLoF [15]          Automatically generates various hierarchical combinations of locks and selects the most performant configuration.
               20 Nap [62]           Introduce NUMA-aware layer over existing persistent memory (PM) indexes to manage hot items and avoid costly remote PM access.
  Hardware




               21 FAERY [66]         Adopt FPGA to accelerate embedding-based retrieval system which requires both high memory bandwidth and pipeline parallelism.
               22 KV-Direct [40]     Use programmable NICs to extend RDMA primitives and directly handle key-value operations in the host memory.
               23 The nanoPU [29] Route incoming messages directly to the running threads’ registers, bypassing traditional memory hierarchies.

                   P+O      Traditional caching policies focus on object hit rate, but transactional workloads need to cache all concurrently requested objects to
                            reduce latency. Transactions modeled as DAGs require scoring for eviction, which is costly, infeasible, and complicated by overlapping
                            object usage.
                  GPT-4     Design a caching policy that prioritizes key groups in transactional DAGs, leveraging runtime heuristics to balance latency and
  DeToX                     computational complexity.
  [12]           SysGPT     Infer transactional DAGs using dynamic profiling to capture transaction locality ( 6 ). Pre-fill the cache with keys ( 3 ) based on
                            dependency tracking.
                 Solution   To limit the number of groups scored, keys interchangeable in reducing critical length are treated as one group. Dynamically infer
                            groups when DAGs are inaccessible ( 6 ). Preemptively cache related items based on dependency tracking ( 3 ).
                   P+O      Relational databases rely on strict monotonicity, while vector systems use approximate top-K, lacking this property. This division forces
                            hybrid queries, like finding top-K vectors meeting relational conditions, to handle similarity search and relational filtering separately,
                            resulting in inefficiencies.
                  GPT-4     Dynamically adjust indices based on query patterns and embedding techniques. Employ adaptive sampling strategies to balance
  VBASE                     precision and computation. Integrate scalar and vector constraints to minimize computational overhead.
  [67]           SysGPT     Integrate vector search with relational databases by developing a query engine tailored for hybrid workloads ( 8 ). Cache tentative
                            results to avoid redundant computation ( 2 ) while incrementally exploring new data. Use an adaptive search model that allows early
                            termination based on the size of the result set during the search ( 6 ).
                 Solution   Instead of having two separate phases—one for finding top-K vectors and another for applying relational query filters—unify these
                            steps into a single execution engine ( 8 ) that incrementally expands traversal and terminates early once the query conditions are met.
                            Use runtime information to traverse high-quality indices more frequently ( 6 ).
                   P+O      The introduction of persistent cache challenges existing designs of online transaction processing engines on non-volatile memory.
                            Cache-NVM granularity mismatch causes write amplification, and out-of-place updates increase NVM writes and require frequent
                            index updates.
                  GPT-4     Eliminate traditional logging by ensuring atomic updates directly in persistent cache. Employ fine-grained in-place updates to minimize
  Falcon                    NVM writes and integrate cache-aware index structures.
  [30]           SysGPT     Eliminate explicit cache line flushing by introducing persistent cache ( 7 ). Set different lifetimes for hot/cold data by stroing them
                            separately in cache ( 2 ). Align cache eviction policies with NVM write block sizes ( 1 ).
                 Solution   With persistent cache, no need to explicitly flush logs for persistency ( 7 ). To reduce write amplification from granularity mismatch,
                            multiple cache lines are merged into one NVM write ( 1 ). A small LRU cache absorbs hot tuples, avoiding manual flushing and reducing
                            NVM writes ( 2 ).
                   P+O      Updating high-dimensional vector indices is challenging due to the cost of maintaining index quality during frequent updates. Existing
                            methods rely on costly periodic global rebuilds, result in fluctuating query latency and accuracy.
                  GPT-4     Adopt a hybrid approach combining cluster-based local updates with lightweight graph pruning. Cluster-based indexing minimizes the
  SPFresh                   cost of local modifications, while periodic, asynchronous graph pruning ensures global quality without frequent full rebuilds.
  [64]           SysGPT     Incrementally update graph indices with minimal distortion on global indices ( 5 ). Only manage short range connections accurately at
                            runtime ( 6 ) and move partition maintenance tasks off the critical search path ( 3 ). Batch updates locally ( 1 ).
                 Solution   Perform incremental updates by reassessing only vectors affected by local changes, rather than rebalancing the entire index ( 5 ).
                            Accumulate small updates locally in partitions ( 1 ) and use existing centroids and data distribution to expedite rebalancing ( 2 ). Move
                            the background split-reassign off from the critical path of update ( 3 ).
                   P+O      Existing systems rely on two-phase commit for atomicity, causing performance limitations due to high RPC and log flushing latencies.
                            Modern hardware with µs-level latency alleviates these issues, shifting the bottleneck to disk read. This creates contention during
                            lock-holding periods, particularly under high workloads.
                  GPT-4     Implement an in-memory caching layer for frequently accessed data. Leverage low-latency storage and fast RPCs to asynchronously
  Chardo-
  nnay                      synchronize disk-based storage.
  [17]           SysGPT     Relax synchronization for reads and eliminate dependencies between transactions ( 6 ). Preemptively aggregate information about
                            transaction participants and prefetch data ( 3 ). Group read and write operations requesting same locks ( 1 , 6 ).
                 Solution   Use fast RPCs to read a counter for strict serializability without locks ( 7 ). Dry run transactions to approximate read sets and prefetch
                            them ( 3 ). Reorder lock acquisition order based on the precomputed read/write sets to avoid deadlocks ( 6 ).
                   P+O      Scaling in-memory databases on multi-core architectures is hindered by contention on range-index structures like B+ trees, caused by
                            synchronous updates for consistency. However, range scans typically operate on stale data and read a few records.
                  GPT-4     Decouple updates and reads by leveraging append-only logs for write operations. Large read-only range scans can bypass the index to
  ScaleDB                   directly access the underlying data.
  [50]           SysGPT     Decouple range index into staging buffers for front-end and backend index update ( 8 ). Apply index updates in batches while caching
                            them in the staging buffers ( 1 , 2 ). Delay updating index from the critical path of transaction processing ( 4 ).
                 Solution   Decouple transaction execution from updating the affected range index ( 8 ). Asynchronously apply batched updates to range indexes
                            with optimistic concurrencty control ( 1 , 4 ). Cache recently committed transactions separately ( 2 ).
  Trubo [36]       P+O      The goal of the paper is user privacy, which is out of our scope.

USENIX Association                        19th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation           427
benchmarks against both a baseline IBM Qiskit configura-
tion and various HyperQ scheduling policies, and scripts to
retrieve and analyze the performance data, including through-
put, utilization, and fidelity. It allows for a comprehensive
validation of the claims made in this paper.

Scope
This artifact is designed to validate the performance claims of
the HyperQ system. Specifically, it allows for the reproduction
of the results in table 3, 4, 6, and figure 10. README.md
provides instructions to run the baseline benchmarks using the
default IBM scheduler and HyperQ benchmarks with three
distinct scheduling policies.

Contents
The artifact consists of Python scripts for core HyperQ
functionalities (such as HypervisorBackend.py) and for
executing the various benchmarks. Scripts dedicated to
data retrieval and result analysis are organized into the
getdata/ and analysis/ directories, respectively. The
benchmark_result/ directory is used for storing bench-
mark workload files and experimental outcomes, and includes
the result_ideal.txt file which provides pre-computed
ideal state vectors.

Hosting
The artifact is hosted on GitHub https://github.com/
1640675651/HyperQ with branch main and commit hash
a1c7460. Future updates will be pushed to the main branch,
and we encourage you to use the latest version available.

Requirements
The artifact was developed and tested on a standard Linux
environment. It requires several software dependencies for its
operation: Qiskit, the Qiskit Aer simulator, and the QASM-
Bench benchmark suite. Additionally, a valid IBM Quantum
Account with an API token is essential for submitting jobs to
IBM’s quantum hardware and retrieving results. For complete
and detailed instructions on how to set up these dependencies
and configure the necessary environment, please consult the
README.md file provided in the artifact’s GitHub repository.

                                                                   Error mitigator. To increase the fidelity of quantum pro-
We propose QOS, an operating system for quantum com-               grams, the error mitigator applies pre- and post-processing
puting. In this context, we define a quantum operating             error mitigation techniques. However, there exists an
system as a software layer that transparently manages              abundance of such techniques, and they typically incur

tradeoffs between conflicting objectives; specifically, users           does not include utilization in the scheduling decisions [62].

7     Limitation
Next, we discuss the limitations of our analysis. Our limita-
tions are due to the trace contents captured by NDTimeline,
and we plan to address these limitations in future work.
Limitations due to data captured by NDTimeline. ND-
Timeline performs coarse-grained profiling and records time
taken by a microbatch’s forward and backward computation.
It is challenging to use this information to analyze stragglers
that occur within a TP or CP group, because TP and CP groups
synchronize, and stragglers at the TP or CP granularity show
up as slow microbatches in our traces. As a result, if the strag-                       (b) Stage partitioning imbalance
gler slows down all microbatches, our method of estimating
idealized microbatch durations will not allow us to compute
the ideal straggler-free execution time, and thus we cannot
analyze the effect of such stragglers.
    A second limitation is due to a bug in NDTimeline which
affects some of our traces. This bug caused NDTimeline to
not record some operations, resulting in simulating the launch                       (c) Sequence length imbalance
of some forward- and backward-compute operations earlier                  Figure 14: Heatmap patterns with different root causes.
incorrectly. The bug was spotted after we had begun collecting
traces, and we post-processed traces affected by this bug to        parallelism; 28% were discarded because the job had too few
fix this problem.                                                   steps to allow analysis;7 and 25% were due to corrupt traces.

A     Artifact Appendix
Abstract
This artifact provides the core functionality of the simulator
and the what-if analysis proposed in the paper, including:
    • estimation of overall slowdown S (Eq. 1);
    • estimation of slowdown St attributed to each operation
      type t (Eq. 2);
    • estimation of slowdown Sw attributed to each worker w
      (Eq. 4);
    • computation of characterization metrics MW (Eq. 5) and
      MS for individual worker issues and stage partitioning
      imbalance, respectively;
    • heatmap visualization as in Figure 14; and
    • timeline generation of the simulated ideal trace visualiz-
      able in Perfetto [17].
It also provides three sample traces to demonstrate the usage
of the tool. More details can be found in “README.md”.
Scope
The artifact allows readers to validate if the provided imple-
mentation of the simulator and the what-if analysis match
the description in the paper and if the code is functional and
sufficiently documented.
Contents
The artifact contains the source code of the simulator and
a set of proposed what-if analysis, three sample traces and
their expected analysis result. It also contains a README file
with detailed documentation of the project and step-by-step
instructions to run the analysis using the traces as examples.

Figure 6: End-to-end latency of cold start. The numbers represent the latency of each phase of a Node.js-based function
(nunjucks—rendering the template to HTML), detailed experimental setup can be found in §6. The entire end-to-end start-up
process consists of three main stages: (1) Control-path Interaction. ① BinaryLoad: The runtime shim [22] loads the Catalyzer
engine binary and starts the client process. ② ArgPrepare: The client process prepares fork-related parameters and invokes
the seed sandbox. (2) Container Initialization. ① Clone: The seed sandbox invokes the clone() syscall to fork a new sandbox.
② RuntimeRecover: The forked sandbox initializes the Go runtime. ③ LogRedirect: The stdout and stderr of the sandbox are
redirected. ④ CtrlRecreate: The sandbox recreates the control server. ⑤ PlatformReload: The sandbox transitions from VMX
root mode to VMX non-root mode. ⑥ KernelUnpause: The guest OS is unpaused to resume execution. ⑦ NetworkPrepare: The
client process prepares the network interface and creates a raw socket that binds to this network interface, then sends the raw
socket to the sandbox. ⑧ InitStack: The guest OS initializes the network stack. ⑨ InstallSeccomp: The sandbox parses and installs
a seccomp filter. ⑩ Activate: The sandbox is attached to the host cgroups and mounts the rootfs. (3) User Code Execution. ①
InitCode: The sandbox loads the appropriate language runtime, compiles the user code, and also loads the function’s dependency
framework and libraries. ② Execute: The sandbox executes user code and provides a response.

                                                                      an in-depth analysis of existing solutions, we identify three
Optimizations for Cold Start. Besides Catalyzer [28], other           key bottlenecks: (1) inefficient control-path interactions, (2)
techniques also adopt fork-based methods [27, 68, 90, 96] to          resource contention under concurrency, and (3) user code ini-
optimize cold start, but often overlook end-to-end life cycle         tialization overhead. To mitigate these issues, we propose
gaps in production environments. These gaps are relevant to           AFaaS. AFaaS replaces the heavyweight OCI with an ef-
various cold start technologies, including lightweight virtu-         ficient FRI in the control path, pools and shares resources
alization [5, 31, 40, 58, 64], unikernels [50, 53, 71, 85], new       to alleviate contention, and uses tree-structured seeds with
container types [24,52,86], container C/R [13,19,28,38,51,55,         multi-level forking for fast forks and efficient memory use.

                                                                  by the AAs. The AAs are identical and run in parallel. Each
                                                                  AA can only process one request at a time, and no preemptions
                                                                  are allowed. Requests cannot be dropped, and each AA has a
                                                                  queue with enough space to hold its pending requests; queued
                                                                  requests are processed in FIFO order.

                                                                  extent of which depends on how much of the request is cached

                                                                  the same portion of the cache (i.e., rules) may help differ-
                                                                  ent requests. In addition, even with the same cache state, the

   We design a type infrastructure to model and mediate safe
interactions with foreign code. This closely relates to work          Software written in type-safe and memory-safe programming
on Linking Types, which seek to extend the type system of a           languages has to interact with components written in foreign,
host language to encode the behaviors and semantics native            unsafe languages. A single violation of the language’s safety
to guest (foreign) code [13, 32, 33, 34, 45]. Existing work           invariants can infringe upon the application’s overall safety.
on linking types is focused primarly on the core semantic                This paper presents Omniglot, a system that preserves
questions or type system development, attempting to express           soundness of host code in the presence of untrusted foreign
foreign semantic guarantees within a host’s type system. How-         code. We demonstrate Omniglot’s generality and low over-
ever, these contributions assume that foreign code is internally      heads by evaluating it on two systems and a diverse set of
correct. Omniglot can safely interact with libraries without          libraries. We show that Omniglot can safely encapsulate for-
reasoning about whether they are correct.                             eign libraries with minimal overheads.
   Finally, verification based approaches like eBPF [24, 28],
promise safe interactions with untrusted code, with only few
or no runtime checks. While these tools are growing increas-
ingly capable and are used in complex settings such as stor-          Acknowledgments

approach, KRR incurs low overhead on the VM performance              [9] DPDK. https://www.dpdk.org/. Last accessed:

                                                                    [10] f-stack. https://github.com/F-Stack/f-stack.

                                                                         Last accessed: November, 2024.
the guest user space. The evaluation shows that KRR achieves
high recording performance on several real-world workloads,         [11] GDB Reverse Debugging. https://sourceware.o

based scheduling techniques for various XPUs, including           ture, advanced XPUs to achieve optimal performance while

24, 63, 67, 133], and FPGAs [57, 65, 69, 104]. Some are           have adapted XSched to various XPU platforms and de-

fast kernel preemption [22, 73, 101] or efficient spatial shar-   with flexible policies. Our experimental evaluation and case
ing [124, 133]. XSched is orthogonal to these techniques, and     studies demonstrate the efficacy and efficiency of XSched
the multi-level hardware model allows XSched to integrate         and its novel techniques. XSched, with its diverse XPU
these hardware enhancements. Some other work enhances the         implementations, is open-source and publicly available at

Implication-6: Modern GPU APIs are already stateless
and can support parallel tasks. The next-generation GPU
APIs such as Vulkan [34], Metal [20], and DirectX12 [8], on
which state-of-the-art rendering services and 2D engines are
built, are stateless within the GPU driver. In contrast with
traditional APIs like OpenGL [23] which maintain a single-
threaded state machine model within the GPU driver, they
delegate the management of GPU objects to the API users.
This provides a necessary condition for scalable and parallel
rendering in multi-core configurations.                            Figure 3: Display specifications of flagship smartphones.

GPU resource management. GPU resources in Spade2D
are managed by thread-safe managers that prevent resource
double creation caused by parallel rendering. Similar to other
2D engines, Spade2D tracks GPU resources needed for vari-
ous rendering algorithms, including buffers, images, pipelines,
shaders, descriptors, etc. These resources are shared among        Figure 9: Representative scenarios rendered by Spars.
rendering tasks and reused across frames if possible, each
of which has a manager using size-class-based pools, hash
tables, circular queues tied to the frame buffer rotation, etc.
Thread safety. In Spade2D, operations on these data struc-
tures need to be thread-safe. However, note that modern state-
less GPU APIs, such as Vulkan [34], Metal [20], and Di-
rectX12 [8], allow the parallelization of actual resource usage
and creation within each rendering task. Time-consuming op-       Figure 10: Execution time proportion of a frame in Spars.
erations like vertex and index buffer filling, image decoding
and creation, and GPU pipeline creation can all be executed       We run Spars with Spade2D on state-of-the-art commercial

source reading, ensuring no contention when multiple render-      fold) [16], and Mate XT (tri-fold) [17], as well as multi-screen
ing tasks refer to the same created GPU object (e.g., pipeline    configurations using the Kirin 9010 chipset [54].
or image). Thus, the cost of synchronization is minimized and

Figure 1: Transformer architecture. The operations in the yellow boxes have large batch sizes and share model weight parameters
across requests; hence, they are compute-bound. Operations in green boxes require loading a unique KV cache for each request;
hence, they are memory-bound. The blue box represents network operations that perform synchronization between operations.

9   Related Work
                                                                    10    Conclusion
Distributed LLM Training Frameworks: To address the
challenges of training extra-large LLMs, prior approaches           In this paper, we present WLB-LLM, a workload-balanced
primarily rely on 3D parallelism [15, 26, 38, 40, 43, 44, 55],      4D parallelism framework designed to enhance the efficiency
which integrates tensor parallelism [15, 17, 38], pipeline par-     of LLM training. WLB-LLM systematically identifies and
allelism [11, 19, 21, 26], and data parallelism [35, 36, 54]. Al-   addresses workload imbalances that arise across multiple par-
though 3D parallelism has proven its effectiveness in scaling       allelism hierarchies. At the pipeline parallelism level, WLB-
model size, enabling the training of models with trillions of       LLM introduces a novel heuristic variable-length document
parameters [40], it struggles to scale context window size          packing algorithm combined with an outlier document delay
effectively. To address this limitation, a new dimension of par-    method that effectively mitigates workload imbalance across
allelism called context parallelism has been introduced [30],       micro-batches. At the context parallelism level, WLB-LLM
forming the 4D parallelism training paradigm. Context paral-        proposes a fine-grained per-document sharding method with
lelism splits input sequences into chunks, effectively reducing     an adaptive sharding selection strategy to maximize CP train-
the memory bottleneck associated with extremely long doc-           ing efficiency. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that
uments. Initially, context parallelism employs a ring-based         WLB-LLM outperforms existing 4D parallelism frameworks
approach that overlaps communication and computation using          across various model sizes and parallelism configurations,
P2P communication [24]. More recent approaches leverage             achieving an average speedup of 1.23×.
collective communication methods (e.g., AllGather or All-
toAll) to aggregate key and value tensors, offering greater
flexibility and better support for various types of attention       11    Acknowledgments
masks [6, 12, 30]. The introduction of context parallelism
enables efficient training of LLMs with long context win-

A    Artifact Appendix

Abstract
Our artifact provides an open-source implementation of the
context parallelism optimization of WLB-LLM. It includes
both the Per-Sequence baseline and the Per-Document shard-
ing optimization proposed by WLB-LLM. This implementa-
tion differs from the internal version used at Meta. We de-
velop this open-source version following the design proposed
in WLB-LLM, using open-source frameworks. The goal is to
make it easier for readers to experiment with and build upon
the context parallelism optimizations presented in WLB-LLM.

Scope
This artifact provides a user-friendly interface to perform
context parallelism training using both Per-Sequence and Per-
Document sharding strategies. It enables quick performance
comparisons between the two approaches, supporting the
claims made in the WLB-LLM paper. It also serves as a good
starting point for exploring further optimizations in context
parallelism.

Contents
The repository includes the following components:
 1. Implementation of both Per-Sequence and Per-
    Document sharding.
 2. Code and scripts for verifying correctness.

 3. Code and scripts for benchmarking the training effi-
    ciency of Per-Sequence vs. Per-Document sharding.
 4. A detailed README.md with usage instructions and setup
    guidance.

Hosting
The artifact is open-sourced on GitHub at: https://github.
com/Ash-Zheng/WLB-LLM-CP. We are actively maintaining
the main branch of the repository to make it more comprehen-
sive. Clear and accessible documentation will be continuously
updated to reflect new features and improvements.

Requirements
We have tested and evaluated our artifact using the
nvcr.io/nvidia/pytorch:25.01-py3 Docker image, with
PyTorch 2.6.0, FlashAttention 2.4.2, and CUDA 12.8. Our
implementation has been validated on both NVIDIA A100
and H100 GPUs. To run performance comparisons between
Per-Sequence and Per-Document sharding, a minimum of two
GPUs is required.

  3 pub open spec fn chunk_corresponds(s1: Seq<u8>, s2: Seq<u8>, chunk: int) -> bool {
  4    forall |i: int| 0 <= i < s1.len() && i / chunk_size() == chunk ==> s1[i] == s2[i]

  6 pub open spec fn can_result_from_partial_write(

  7    post: Seq<u8>, pre: Seq<u8>, addr: int, bytes: Seq<u8>) -> bool
  8 {

  9    post.len() == pre.len() && forall |chunk| {
 10       ||| chunk_corresponds(post, pre, chunk)
 11       ||| chunk_corresponds(post, update_bytes(pre, addr, bytes), chunk)
 12 }}

 16      &&& can_result_from_partial_write(self.durable_state, pre.durable_state, addr, bytes)

  1 pub open spec fn maybe_corrupted(self, bytes: Seq<u8>, true_bytes: Seq<u8>, addrs: Seq<int>) -> bool {
  2   &&& bytes.len() == true_bytes.len() == addrs.len()
  3   &&& forall |i: int| 0 <= i < bytes.len()
  4     ==> exists |mask: u8| bytes[i] == (true_bytes[i] ^ (mask & self.corruption[addrs[i]]))
  5 }

  6 pub exec fn read(&self, addr: u64, num_bytes: u64) -> (bytes: Vec<u8>)

  7   requires self.inv(), addr + num_bytes <= self@.len(),
  8   ensures ({
  9     let true_bytes = self@.read_state.subrange(addr as int, addr + num_bytes);
 10     let addrs = Seq::<int>::new(true_bytes.len(), |i: int| i+addr);
 11     self.constants().maybe_corrupted(bytes@, true_bytes, addrs) })

                           Abstract
   The Okapi cluster file system decouples how data is spread
across disks (data striping) for IO efficiency from how data is
erasure coded together (redundancy grouping) for durability.
Existing systems couple these two mechanisms’ configura-                       (a) Coupled: 4-of-6 grouping implies 4-wide striping
tions, inducing significant inefficiencies. Decoupling allows
grouping to be configured based on reliability and space ef-
ficiency goals, while simultaneously allowing striping to be
configured based on performance goals. Decoupling also al-
lows redundancy scheme changes from one EC scheme to
                                                                          (b) Decoupled: 6-of-8 grouping while choosing 4-wide striping
another (e.g., to react to data temperature or disk failure rate
changes) to occur without having to re-write data. Evaluation       Figure 1: 1a shows a file in a coupled architecture with a 4-of-6 EC scheme

Although Compass uses an HNSW graph as the underlying
data structure rather than a tree, Compass ensures that each
node’s data, including the coordinates and neighbor list, is
stored inside one of the buckets that form a binary tree on
the server side. Therefore, the properties of the Merkle hash
tree apply directly, which means that the probability of the
server successfully forging a response that passes the client’s
integrity check is negligible.

B     Artifact Appendix                                             both the Docker/Zenodo and GitHub versions of the artifact.

Abstract
Our artifact contains the code for the Paralegal analyzer, pol-
icy compiler, supporting libraries, the set of applications we
evaluate on, the benchmarker used to run evaluations, and the
plotting script to generate the figures in the paper.
Scope
The artifact allows reproducing the following results:
1. Comparison with CodeQL (column three in Figure 8).
2. Policy structure and coding claims (paragraph “Policy
   Structure” in §7.2.2).
3. Bugs found by Paralegal (§7.1).
4. The ergonomics report from §7.3.
5. All claims made in performance evaluations in §7.4, such
   as Figures 9 to 12.
Contents
The artifact contains:
1. Source code for the Paralegal code analyzer, policy com-
   piler, and supporting libraries for annotations and the low-
   level Rust API for policies.
2. The source code for all case study applications mentioned
   in the paper, as well as their Paralegal policies.
3. C++ translations for the case study applications and the
   CodeQL policies we tried on them.
4. Source code for the benchmarker used to run the evalua-
   tions.
5. The plotting script used to generate the figures in the paper.
   The Docker container version of the artifact additionally
contains the CodeQL version we used and all dependencies
needed for any software that runs or is analyzed during the
benchmarks.
Hosting
We provide two versions of the artifact: a Docker image
hosted on Zenodo [3] and a GitHub repository [2] (tag: final).
   The container is intended as an everything-included solu-
tion that allows for validation without any (online) dependen-
cies.
   The GitHub repository contains only the immediate source
code for the programs and use cases, as well as instructions
and lockfiles to replicate the environment used for the evalua-
tion.

A     Artifact Appendix

Abstract
The artifact contains every custom component that is needed
to recreate the measurements presented in the paper. It is a
bundle of source files of the individual projects created for this
paper. This includes the MettEagle software and benchmark
code. However, external, unmodified software (like Linux or
Firecracker) is not included.

Scope
The artifact strives to achieve artifact available. It only
contains source files and some documentation but no
all-in-one script for fitting all the individual projects together.
Thus, this artifact does not claim easy functional evaluation.
Unfortunately, due to the large number of moving parts and
long compilation times, setting up the benchmark environment
takes some time. If any question arise while using the provided
artifact, please contact the authors.
   The artifact contains the code of the MettEagle FaaS
runtime including the surrounding L4Re. It is thus possible
to run MettEagle using this artifact. Furthermore, all the
benchmark scripts for exercising MettEagle are included.
Most importantly, a modified version of the SeBS benchmark
suite is included to run functions on MettEagle. All code used
to create comparative benchmarks on Linux is also included.

Contents
For a precise description of the provided artifacts, please refer
to the README.md inside of the artifact.

Hosting
The artifact is available via Zenodo:                 https:
//doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.15211297.

Requirements
The artifact is designed for the x86-64 architecture. It is tested
to run inside of Qemu and on the machine described in Sec-
tion 6.1. The network benchmarks can either run via emulated
NICs in Qemu or via connecting two physical machines.
